title: Machine learning reveals tropical aerosol-driven cloud expansion despite stronger rainfall
summary: Using satellite observations of four Kīlauea volcanic outgassing episodes in 2008 and 2018, an ML counterfactual analysis found that volcanic aerosols increased cloud cover and reflected sunlight over tropical marine shallow-convective clouds, even as rainfall strengthened. Cloud-cover adjustment contributed about 65% of aerosol–cloud cooling under mixed meteorological conditions and 84–87% in humid conditions; under humid, stable conditions, a 30% increase in droplet number could correspond to up to a 50% relative increase in cloud cover. The result identifies a tropical regime in which aerosol cloud expansion is strong and its response varies with humidity and stability.
ai_technology: Random-forest machine-learning surrogates of MODIS cloud properties, radiative fluxes, and precipitation, trained on 20 years of satellite observations and meteorology while excluding volcanic years 2008 and 2018
organization: University of Exeter; Met Office; ETH Zurich; NASA Goddard Space Flight Center; University of Cambridge; University of Leeds; University of Reading

evidence.tested: Using satellite observations of four Kīlauea volcanic outgassing episodes in 2008 and 2018, an ML counterfactual analysis found that volcanic aerosols increased cloud cover and reflected sunlight over tropical marine shallow-convective clouds, even as rainfall strengthened.
evidence.unknown: This is an observational ML-counterfactual analysis of four Kīlauea plume months over tropical marine shallow-convective clouds, not a controlled aerosol intervention or a direct test of deliberate cloud seeding. The source reports strong cloud-cover responses and radiative estimates, especially under humid/stable conditions, but results depend on satellite retrievals and the learned unperturbed baseline. The authors’ proposed mechanism for increased cloud cover alongside stronger rainfall is explicitly a hypothesis requiring further testing; do not treat the marine-cloud-brightening scenario as experimentally demonstrated.
evidence.ai_role: The random-forest surrogates estimated unperturbed cloud properties and radiative fluxes for given meteorological conditions. Comparing those counterfactuals with observations in four volcanic plume episodes isolated aerosol-associated signals from meteorological co-variability and enabled estimates of cloud-cover, rainfall, and radiative-forcing responses across distinct tropical meteorological regimes.
